patent: Filed March 23, 1903 and issued January 5, 1904 to Lizzie J. Magie of Brentwood, Maryland; no assignee. The text names the game "The landlord's game". Players circle a square track of lots for sale or rent, railroads, light and water franchises, taxed necessities and luxuries, a jail and a poorhouse, and draw wages each time they pass the starting corner; the winner holds the most lots, cash and luxuries after an agreed number of circuits. Magie was a follower of Henry George's single-tax economics (Progress and Poverty, 1879), and the rules carry that argument: "No trespassing" spaces are "property held out of use", and the flat charge on necessities "represents indirect taxation". The game is widely regarded as the forerunner of Monopoly, which Parker Brothers published in 1935 credited to Charles Darrow; that year Parker Brothers also bought her patent on a revised version (Elizabeth Magie Phillips, US 1,509,312, 1924). Source for the history: Mary Pilon, The Monopolists, Bloomsbury, 2015.

figs.1: Plan of the board, turned so the "Fig. 1" label reads upright; the lettering along each side faces a different way. Nine spaces run along each side between four corners: start (the globe, "Labor upon mother earth produces wages") at bottom right, the barred jail with the coal tax at bottom left, the poorhouse and public park at top left, and the "No trespassing / Go to jail" estate of "Lord Blueblood" at top right. Lots 1 to 22 run clockwise from the start, each marked with its rent and a sale price ten times the rent; a railroad sits mid-side on every side. The four central squares hold the Bank, Railroad, Public Treasury and Wages boxes. The "2" inside the globe and the "T" in the railroad square are not explained in the text.
figs.2: One piece of each set, drawn in perspective with heavy shade lines on the lower and right edges. Rectangles are the paper tickets (note 29, mortgage 30, bank mortgage 31, charter 32, deed 28, luxury 33, legacy 34, and lot ticket 25 bearing lot number 1); 26 is a die, 27 the dice cup, 35 a $50 money chip and 36 a plain round checker. The box at lower left belongs to Fig. 3.
figs.3: One of the four central boxes, here the Bank, as a lidded box seen from above at an angle; the heavy line marks the lid's lower edge and the vertical hatching shades the end face.

parts.24: One of four boxes (Bank, Wages, Public treasury, Railroad) placed in the four central spaces of the board.
parts.25: Twenty-two lot tickets, one per lot space; at the start each player draws tickets and may buy the matching lots.
parts.30: Placed by a lending player on top of the borrower's deed to mark the loan.
parts.36: The text gives four checkers "to check the throws made"; the rules also keep a tally-sheet of circuits.

glossary.def: Henry George's proposal to replace other taxes with a single tax on the rental value of land.
Taxes collected on goods, such as excise duties and tariffs, and paid by consumers through higher prices rather than levied on them directly.
A public grant giving a company the exclusive right to supply a service such as light or water.
The document granting a franchise; in the game a player places it on a franchise space to claim it.
The document of title to a piece of land.
A promissory note: a signed promise to repay a loan.
A claim on property given as security for a loan.
Money or property left to someone in a will.
A publicly funded institution housing people who could not support themselves.
Patent-drawing convention: edges facing away from a light assumed at the upper left are drawn heavier, so raised objects read as solid.
Sheet-header note that the application was filed without a working model.
